data.name: Guide_Intro
data.value: How each FFmpeg receive option affects latency and reliability. The defaults favor real-time while staying robust on most sources; raise the buffers if you see green bands or stutter on a high-bitrate stream.

data.name: OptHelp_transport_Tip
data.value: How RTP is carried: Auto (UDP, TCP fallback), UDP only, or TCP only.

data.name: OptHelp_transport_Body
data.value: Chooses the RTSP lower transport. UDP has the lowest latency but drops packets on a busy or lossy network, which shows up as green bands and corruption. TCP is reliable (no packet loss) at the cost of a little latency — the best choice for high-bitrate streams or networks you don't control. Auto starts on UDP and falls back to TCP only if no frame arrives at all.

data.name: OptHelp_hwdecode_Tip
data.value: Decode on the GPU (d3d11va) when available; off forces software decoding.

data.name: OptHelp_hwdecode_Body
data.value: When on, H.264/H.265 are decoded on the GPU (Direct3D 11 / DXVA), which is much cheaper for high-resolution streams and keeps latency down. Turn it off if a GPU driver misbehaves (artifacts, crashes) to fall back to CPU decoding.

data.name: OptHelp_sockettimeout_Tip
data.value: How long to wait on the RTSP socket before giving up (milliseconds).

data.name: OptHelp_sockettimeout_Body
data.value: Maps to FFmpeg's stimeout. Bounds how long a stalled connection blocks before the engine retries, and how long a dead UDP attempt waits before Auto falls back to TCP. Too low can abort a slow-but-alive source; too high makes a truly dead source hang longer before reconnecting.

data.name: OptHelp_reorder_Tip
data.value: How many out-of-order RTP packets to hold before dropping them.

data.name: OptHelp_reorder_Body
data.value: Maps to FFmpeg's reorder_queue_size. On UDP, packets can arrive out of order; a larger window lets the engine wait for them instead of dropping them, which is what prevents missing slices (green bands) on a high-bitrate stream. Set too low it shreds a busy stream; very high can add latency during loss. Irrelevant on TCP.

data.name: OptHelp_buffersize_Tip
data.value: Size of the UDP receive buffer, in KB. Larger absorbs high-bitrate bursts.

data.name: OptHelp_buffersize_Body
data.value: Maps to FFmpeg's buffer_size (the socket receive buffer). A full 1080p frame of incompressible video arrives as a burst of many packets; if the buffer is too small the OS silently drops the overflow, causing green bands. A few MB absorbs the burst. This — together with the reorder window — is the main fix for packet loss on UDP even when bandwidth is plentiful. 0 leaves the system default.

data.name: OptHelp_maxdelay_Tip
data.value: Extra time the demuxer may wait to reorder packets (milliseconds).

data.name: OptHelp_maxdelay_Body
data.value: Maps to FFmpeg's max_delay. 0 emits each frame as soon as it's decoded (lowest latency). A small non-zero value gives the reorder buffer time to wait for late packets, trading a little latency for smoother playback on a jittery network.

data.name: OptHelp_latencycap_Tip
data.value: If the picture falls this far behind live, jump back to live (milliseconds).

data.name: OptHelp_latencycap_Body
data.value: This is our own resync-to-live guard, not an FFmpeg option. If a decoded frame is more than this many milliseconds behind real time (a slow decoder, or a bursty source building a backlog), the engine drops to the next keyframe to catch up. Lower keeps latency tight but causes more visible jumps; higher is smoother but laggier.
